pack.title: Unit 6.0 Configuring Network Addressing and Internet Connections

flashcards.definition: Internet access that uses the higher frequencies of copper telephone lines; the modem's RJ11 port connects to the phone point, and a filter (splitter) in each phone socket separates voice and data.
Internet access that usually comes as part of a cable access TV (CATV) service, over a hybrid fiber coax (HFC) network: a fiber optic core with copper coax links to customer premises.
The device that connects to the local router through an RJ45 port and to the provider's network through a short segment of coax with threaded F-type connectors.
Internet access that brings fiber optic links into the last mile; with fiber to the premises (FTTP), the provider's fiber optic cable runs all the way to the customer's building.

reference.title: Fiber to the Curb and Fiber to the Premises

flashcards.definition: The device at the customer's premises that terminates the provider's fiber and converts the optical signal to an electrical one; it connects to the router with an RJ45 patch cord.

reference.title: Fiber to the Curb and Fiber to the Premises

flashcards.definition: Internet access by microwave radio to satellites, covering far bigger areas than other types; high geostationary orbit adds a lot of latency, while low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites have less.

A provider of ground-based, long-range fixed wireless internet access through a directional antenna at the customer's site; the link needs a clear line of sight and usually has lower latency than satellite.
Internet access through a cellular radio that connects to the closest base station, whose service area is called a cell; 4G (LTE) and 5G can also be fixed wireless broadband for homes and businesses.
A device with interfaces in two or more networks, such as the private LAN and the public WAN, that forwards packets between networks using IP addresses.
Filters which hosts and protocols can pass, using rules called an access control list (ACL) that allow or block traffic by network address and protocol type.
A 32-bit address written in dotted decimal notation: four octets, each a number from 0 to 255, separated by periods, such as 192.168.0.1.
A 32-bit value, such as 255.255.255.0 (/24), whose 1 bits mark the network ID part of an IPv4 address; the remaining bits are the host ID.
The IP address of a router interface, in the same IP network as the host, that the host uses to forward packets to other networks.

An IPv4 address from a reserved range (10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255, 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, or 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255) that is confined to LANs and cannot route traffic over the Internet.
A unique address, allocated to the customer's network by the ISP, that a host needs to communicate on the Internet, such as the address of a SOHO router's interface to the ISP.
An IP address an administrator types in by hand on each host; typically used only for systems with a dedicated function, such as router interfaces or servers that need a fixed address.

reference.title: Static Versus Dynamic Host Address Configuration

flashcards.definition: An IP address a host receives automatically from a DHCP server instead of having an administrator type it in by hand.

reference.title: Static Versus Dynamic Host Address Configuration

flashcards.definition: A 169.254 address a host gives itself at random when it is set to use DHCP but cannot contact a DHCP server; with it, the host cannot reach other networks.

reference.title: Static Versus Dynamic Host Address Configuration

flashcards.definition: A 128-bit address written in hexadecimal as eight 16-bit groups separated by colons; the first 64 bits are the network ID and the last 64 bits identify the interface.
The connection-oriented transport protocol: it opens a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK), numbers each packet, and can recover from lost or out-of-order packets.
The connectionless transport protocol with no sequencing or acknowledgments; its lower overhead makes it faster, so it suits time-sensitive data such as voice and video.
Makes files available for download across a network; TCP port 20 for the data connection and TCP port 21 for the control connection.
Makes a secure connection to the command-line interface of a server; TCP port 22.
Makes an unsecure connection to the command-line interface of a server; TCP port 23.
Sends (transfers) email messages across a network; TCP port 25.
Delivers unsecure (unencrypted) websites and web services; TCP port 80.
Retrieves email messages from a server mailbox; TCP port 110.
NetBIOS over TCP/IP supports the networking features of legacy Windows versions; UDP and TCP ports 137 to 139.
Reads and manages mail messages on a server mailbox; TCP port 143.
Queries information about network users and resources; TCP port 389.
Delivers secure (encrypted) websites and services; TCP port 443.

flashcards.term: SMB/CIFS (Server Message Block/Common Internet File System)
flashcards.definition: Provides Windows-compatible file and printer sharing services on a local network; TCP port 445.
Makes a secure connection to the graphical desktop of a computer; TCP port 3389.
Lets a server give hosts their IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers automatically; the server listens on UDP port 67 and the client on UDP port 68.
The range of IP addresses a DHCP server can offer to client hosts in a particular subnet, such as 192.168.0.100 to 192.168.0.199.
An address left out of the DHCP scope because a device already uses it as a static address, such as the SOHO router's own LAN address.

A DHCP server's assignment of an IP address to a client for a limited period only; the client tries to renew it before it expires, and if it cannot, it must release the address and start discovery again.
A DHCP server setting that ties a host's MAC address to a particular IP address, so that host receives the same address every time it joins the network.
Resolves host and domain names to IP addresses, so hosts can be found by name; TCP and UDP port 53.
The DNS record that resolves a host name to an IPv4 address.
The DNS record that resolves a host name to an IPv6 address.
The DNS record that links one domain name to another domain name, such as sending visitors of an acquired company's website to the new owner's site.
The DNS record that identifies an email server for the domain so other servers can send it messages; when there are several, the lowest preference value is preferred.
The DNS record that stores free-form text for other network services; most often used to verify email services and block spoofed and unwanted messages (spam).
The TXT record, only one per domain, that lists the hosts authorized to send email from that domain.
Publishes a public encryption key as a TXT record so receiving organizations can use cryptography to verify that a message came from an authentic server for the domain.
The TXT record policy that makes sure SPF and DKIM are used effectively, sets how failures are treated (flag, quarantine, or reject), and lets receivers report failures to the sender.
A managed switch feature that divides its ports into logical groups, each with its own subnet, to reduce broadcast traffic and improve security; traffic between groups must go through a router.
A protected, encrypted tunnel through the Internet that lets an authenticated remote host join the LAN as if it were on site; it can also link branch offices to a head office.
